p.src: Now when Zhang Heng heard that his brother Zhang Shun was dead, grief overwhelmed him and he lay unconscious for a long while before they managed to revive him. Song Jiang said, “Help him into the tent and tend to him. We shall ask him about what happened at sea afterward.” Song Jiang ordered Pei Xuan and Jiang Jing to record the merits of all the commanders, and between the hours of the Dragon and the Snake everyone assembled before the camp. Li Jun and Shi Xiu captured Wu Zhi alive; the three women commanders captured Zhang Daoyuan; Lin Chong speared Leng Gong to death with his serpent spear; and Xie Zhen and Xie Bao killed Cui Yu. Only five men escaped: Shi Bao, Deng Yuanjue, Wang Ji, Chao Zhong, and Wen Kerang. Song Jiang promptly issued proclamations to reassure the people and rewarded the whole army. Wu Zhi and Zhang Daoyuan were sent under guard to Commander Zhang’s headquarters and beheaded. A memorial was submitted recommending Yuan the judicial officer, who had presented the grain, for appointment as magistrate of Fuyang County. A blank patent of office was obtained from Commander Zhang; of this there is no more to tell. The commanders all went into the city to rest. Presently an attendant reported, “Ruan Xiaoqi has come ashore from the river and entered the city.” Song Jiang summoned him before the command tent and questioned him. Ruan Xiaoqi said, “Zhang Heng, Hou Jian, Duan Jingzhu, and I led the sailors in search of vessels along the coast. When we reached the vicinity of Haiyan, we hoped to sail straight into the Qiantang River. But unexpectedly wind and current were against us, and we were driven out into the open sea. We struggled to turn back, but the wind smashed our vessel, and everyone fell into the water. Hou Jian and Duan Jingzhu could not swim; they sank and drowned in the sea. The many sailors scattered, each seeking his own escape. I swam to the mouth of the river and entered through Zheshamen, but the tide swept me straight to Banpan Mountain, from where I swam back. Then I saw Brother Zhang Heng in the river by Wuyun Mountain. He had meant to come ashore, but afterward I did not know where he was. Last night I saw fire rise in the city and heard cannon shots in rapid succession. I supposed that you, Brother, must be fighting inside Hangzhou, so I came ashore from the river. I do not know whether Zhang Heng managed to reach the shore.” Song Jiang told Ruan Xiaoqi what had happened to Zhang Heng, then had him meet his own two elder brothers and resume command of the naval leaders and their vessels. Song Jiang gave orders to dispatch the naval commanders first, so that they might ready the river craft and await the advance on Muzhou. Remembering how Zhang Shun had displayed such divine power as a manifest spirit, Song Jiang had a temple built outside Yongjin Gate beside West Lake, entitled him “Protector of Jinhua,” and went there in person to offer sacrifice. Later, after Fang La had been subdued and meritorious service rendered to the court, Song Jiang returned to the capital and reported the matter. By special imperial decree Zhang Shun was enfeoffed as “General of Jinhua,” and sacrifices were offered to him in Hangzhou.

p.src: Now Song Jiang, while staying in the temporary palace, reflected on how many commanders and officers had been lost since crossing the river, and his heart was filled with grief. He therefore went to Jingci Temple and held a seven-day-and-night Water and Land rite, distributing food offerings to succor souls sunk in darkness and deliver the fallen commanders. Memorial tablets were set up for each of them to receive sacrifice. When these rites were completed, he had every structure in Fang Tianding’s palace demolished, and distributed all the gold, silver, jewels, silks, satins, and other goods among the commanders and officers. The people of Hangzhou were all restored to peace, and a banquet was held in celebration and reward. Song Jiang then made thorough plans with the military adviser to mobilize the army and recover Muzhou. It was now near the end of the fourth month when a sudden report came: “Deputy Commander Liu Guangshi and an imperial envoy from the Eastern Capital have both arrived in Hangzhou.” Song Jiang at once led the commanders out through the northern gate to welcome them into the city. In the temporary palace the imperial edict was opened and read: “…The vanguard commander Song Jiang and his men, having repeatedly rendered great service in suppressing Fang La, are hereby granted by imperial favor thirty-five bottles of wine from the imperial cellars and thirty-five robes of brocade, to be bestowed upon the principal commanders; as for the remaining subordinate commanders, lengths of satin are to be issued as rewards according to the register of their names.” The truth was that the court knew only that Gongsun Sheng had not crossed the river to join the campaign against Fang La; it did not know that so many leaders had been lost. When Song Jiang saw the thirty-five brocade robes and bottles of imperial wine, sorrow suddenly overcame him, and his tears would not cease. When the imperial envoy asked why, Song Jiang told him how the commanders had fallen. The envoy said, “How could the court know that so many commanders had been lost? When this humble official returns to the capital, I shall certainly report it to the throne.” A banquet was then laid to entertain the imperial envoy. Liu Guangshi occupied the seat of honor, while all the other commanders and officers, high and low, sat according to rank. At the banquet they drank the imperial wine, and each man partook of the sovereign’s favor. The brocade robes and imperial wine allotted to the deceased principal and subordinate commanders were set aside. The next day memorial places were prepared, and offerings were made to the departed spirits from afar beneath the open sky. Song Jiang took one bottle of imperial wine and one brocade robe to Zhang Shun’s temple, where he invoked Zhang Shun by name and offered sacrifice. The brocade robe was placed upon the clay image of the god; all the remaining offerings were burned for the spirits from afar. After staying several days, the imperial envoy was escorted back to the capital.

p.src: Time sped by, and before they knew it several dozen days had passed. Commander Zhang sent a man bearing a dispatch urging the vanguard to advance. Song Jiang and Wu Yong invited Lu Junyi to confer with them. “The road from here to Muzhou follows the river straight toward the bandits’ lair; the road from here to Shezhou, however, follows the narrow path through Yuling Pass. We shall divide our forces here for the campaign. Which place would you prefer to attack, worthy brother?” Lu Junyi replied, “The deployment of troops and appointment of commanders are subject to your strict command, Brother. How would I dare choose?” Song Jiang said, “Even so, let us test the will of Heaven.” They fixed the numbers for two divisions and wrote the names of the two destinations on lots. After burning incense and praying, each man drew one. Song Jiang drew Muzhou, while Lu Junyi drew Shezhou. Song Jiang said, “Fang La’s bandit lair lies in Bangyuan Cave in Qingxi County. Once you have taken Shezhou, worthy brother, you may station your army there and send an urgent dispatch to notify me. We shall appoint a day to attack the bandits’ cave at Qingxi together.” Lu Junyi then asked Song Gongming to determine how the commanders, officers, and troops should be divided and deployed.

p.src: Thereupon Vanguard Lu, commanding twenty-nine senior and junior officers and thirty thousand troops and horsemen, chose an auspicious day to take leave of Commander Liu and bid farewell to Song Jiang. He led his army toward Hangzhou by the mountain road, passed through Lin'an County, and continued on his way. Meanwhile, Song Jiang and the others readied their ships, troops, and horses, assigned the senior and junior officers, and chose a day to sacrifice before the standard and march out. The forces advanced by land and water, with ships and cavalry supporting one another. At that time a virulent epidemic was raging within Hangzhou, and six commanders had already fallen ill: Zhang Heng, Mu Hong, Kong Ming, Zhu Gui, Yang Lin, and Bai Sheng. As they had not yet recovered and could not join the campaign, Mu Chun and Zhu Fu were assigned to tend them; thus eight men in all remained behind in Hangzhou. All the remaining commanders accompanied Song Jiang to capture Muzhou—thirty-seven in all—and advanced along the river toward Fuyang County.

p.src: Leaving the two armies to set out, the tale returns to Chai Jin and Yan Qing. After bidding Vanguard Song farewell at Zuili Pavilion in Xiuzhou, they traveled to Haiyan County, reached the coast, took passage by boat past Yuezhou, and proceeded by stages to Zhuji County. They crossed Yupu and came to the border of Muzhou. The officers guarding the pass stopped them. Chai Jin declared, “I am a scholar from the Central Plains. I understand astronomy and geography, am versed in the principles of yin and yang, know the signs of the Six Jia and the winds and clouds, and can distinguish the emanations and hues of the sun, moon, and stars. Of the Nine Schools and Three Teachings there is nothing I do not comprehend. From afar I saw the aura of an emperor over Jiangnan and came here. Why do you bar the road to worthy men?” Hearing that Chai Jin spoke with uncommon distinction, the officers at the pass asked his name. Chai Jin replied, “My surname is Ke and my given name is Yin. Master and servant, we have come to offer our services to your noble realm, and for no other reason.” On hearing this, the garrison commander detained Chai Jin and dispatched a man straight to Muzhou to report before four officials: Right Chancellor Zu Shiyuan, Administrative Councillor Shen Shou, Imperial Secretary Huan Yi, and Marshal Tan Gao. They at once sent men to escort Chai Jin to Muzhou for an audience. After the courtesies had been exchanged, a speech from Chai Jin greatly impressed all four. Moreover, his appearance was anything but ordinary, so they readily harbored no suspicion. Right Chancellor Zu Shiyuan was delighted and ordered Assistant Secretary Huan Yi to conduct Chai Jin to the imperial palace at Qingxi for an audience. It turned out that Fang La maintained traveling palaces and great halls in both Muzhou and Shezhou, while the central offices of the Five Commissions and Six Ministries were located in Bangyuan Cavern in Qingxi County. Chai Jin and Yan Qing followed Huan Yi to the imperial capital at Qingxi, where they first paid their respects to Left Chancellor Lou Minzhong. Chai Jin discoursed eloquently and at length. Lou Minzhong was delighted and kept him as a guest at the chancellor's residence. Seeing that both Chai Jin and Yan Qing spoke with distinction and were learned and courteous, he was already eight parts pleased with them. This Lou Minzhong had originally been a teacher in Qingxi County. Though he possessed some literary learning, it was far from profound; Chai Jin's discourse therefore pleased him enormously. After the night had passed, they attended the morning court next day and waited for Prince Fang La to ascend the throne hall. Within stood the palace attendants, consorts, and palace maidens; outside were arrayed the Nine Ministers and Four Chancellors, the civil and military ranks, and warriors before the hall bearing golden maces in constant attendance. Left Chancellor Lou Minzhong then stepped from the ranks and memorialized: “The Central Plains are the homeland of Master Confucius. A worthy man named Ke Yin has now arrived. Accomplished in both letters and arms and fully endowed with wisdom and courage, he understands astronomy and geography, reads the signs of the Six Jia and the winds and clouds, and comprehends the emanations and hues of Heaven and Earth. The Three Teachings, the Nine Schools, the philosophers, and the Hundred Schools—there is none in which he is not versed. He has come after observing the aura of an emperor. He now waits outside the palace gate for Your Majesty's summons.” Fang La said, “Since a worthy man has arrived, let him come to court in commoner's robes.” The heralds at each gate passed on the summons and conducted Chai Jin below the throne hall. After performing the formal prostrations, offering greetings, and crying “Long live the sovereign!” three times, he was summoned before the curtain. Fang La saw that Chai Jin's appearance was extraordinary, with the bearing of a scion of emperors, and at once looked eight parts pleased. Fang La asked, “You say that you came after observing the aura of an emperor. Where is it to be found?” Chai Jin memorialized: “Your servant Ke Yin was born to humble circumstances in the Central Plains. Both my parents died, and alone I pursued my studies, inheriting the secret arts of former sages and receiving the mystic texts of the patriarchs. Recently, while observing the heavens by night, I saw the Imperial Star shining brightly, directly illuminating Eastern Wu. Therefore, heedless of the hardship of a thousand-li journey, I followed the aura here. Upon reaching Jiangnan, I further saw a wisp of the five-colored aura of an emperor rising from Muzhou. Now that I have beheld Your Majesty's sacred countenance, I see that you possess the form of dragon and phoenix and a presence as exalted as Heaven and the sun, corresponding precisely to that aura. Your servant is overcome with joy and good fortune!” Having spoken, he bowed twice more. Fang La said, “Though We possess a share of the lands of the southeast, Song Jiang and his men have lately seized our cities and are drawing near our territory. What is to be done?” Chai Jin memorialized:

p.src: “Your servant has heard the ancients say: ‘What is easily gained is easily lost; what is gained with difficulty is lost with difficulty.’ Since Your Majesty founded your realm in the southeast, your armies have swept onward unchecked and taken a great many prefectures and commanderies. Though Song Jiang has now seized several places, before long the course of destiny will return to Your Sacred Majesty. Your Majesty shall possess not only the lands of Jiangnan; one day the altars of the realm in the Central Plains shall also be yours.” Fang La was greatly delighted by these words. By imperial decree, Chai Jin was given a brocade-covered stool and ordered to sit. He was entertained at an imperial banquet and additionally appointed Vice Director of the Secretariat. From then on Chai Jin attended Fang La every day, doing nothing but flatter him with pleasing words and fawning upon him to further his purpose. Before half a month had passed, there was not one among Fang La or the officials inside and outside the court who did not like Chai Jin. Later, seeing that Chai Jin handled affairs impartially, Fang La cherished him wholeheartedly. He ordered Left Chancellor Lou Minzhong to act as matchmaker and gave Princess Jinzhi to Chai Jin in a matrilocal marriage, making him an imperial son-in-law and appointing him Commandant of the Imperial Clan. Yan Qing changed his name to Yun Biren, and everyone called him Commandant Yun. After marrying the princess, Chai Jin freely entered and left the palace and learned every detail of its internal and external arrangements. Whenever Fang La had important military affairs to consider, he summoned Chai Jin to the inner palace for consultation. Chai Jin would often memorialize: “Your Majesty's aura is truly that of a sovereign, but it is being assailed by the Stars of the Dipper, so there will yet be six months of unrest. Once every last fighting commander under Song Jiang has been destroyed, the Stars of the Dipper will withdraw from their course. Your Majesty will then restore your great enterprise, sweep onward unchecked, and seize the lands of the Central Plains.” Fang La said, “Several of Our beloved commanders have all been slain by Song Jiang. What is to be done about this?” Chai Jin memorialized again: “Your servant has observed the heavens by night. According to Your Majesty's allotted destiny, though there are scores of General Stars, they do not embody the true vital force and will surely perish before long. Yan Qing changed his name to Yun Biren, and everyone called him Commandant Yun.

p.src: Let us say no more of Chai Jin becoming the imperial son-in-law, but turn instead to Song Jiang, who led his great host away from Hangzhou and advanced toward Fuyang County. There, the Imperial Preceptor Baoguang, Deng Yuanjue, together with Marshal Shi Bao, Wang Ji, Chao Zhong, and Wen Kerang, had brought the remnants of their defeated army to hold the passes of Fuyang County, while sending men to Muzhou to ask for aid. Right Chancellor Zu Shiyuan accordingly dispatched two commanders of the imperial guard with ten thousand troops to reinforce them. The chief commander was Bai Qin and his deputy was Jing De; both possessed courage enough to withstand ten thousand men. On reaching Fuyang County, they joined forces with the Imperial Preceptor Baoguang and the others and occupied the hilltop. Song Jiang's great army had already reached Qiliwan. With the naval forces guiding the cavalry, they all pressed forward together. When Shi Bao saw them, he mounted his horse with his meteor hammer and took up his Wind-Cleaving Saber, then left the hill above Fuyang County to meet Song Jiang. Guan Sheng was just about to ride out when Lü Fang called, “Brother, wait a moment and watch me fight this wretch for a few bouts.” Watching from beneath the shadow of the command banner, Song Jiang saw Lü Fang charge straight at Shi Bao, mounted on his horse and wielding his halberd; Shi Bao met him with the Wind-Cleaving Saber. After the two had fought fifty bouts, Lü Fang began to weaken. Seeing this, Guo Sheng spurred forward with his halberd to join the attack. Yet Shi Bao, with a single saber, fought against both halberds without exposing the slightest opening. Just as the fighting reached its fiercest, the Imperial Preceptor Baoguang to the south urgently sounded the gong for retreat. He had seen warships on the great river riding the following wind upstream toward the shallows and drawing close to the bank. Fearing an attack from two sides, he had therefore sounded the gong to withdraw. But Lü Fang and Guo Sheng kept Shi Bao locked in combat and refused to let him go. After Shi Bao had fought another few bouts, Zhu Tong charged from the Song formation on horseback with his spear and joined the attack. Unable to withstand the three generals, Shi Bao knocked their weapons aside and fled. Song Jiang pointed with the tip of his whip, and his troops charged straight across the hills of Fuyang. Shi Bao's troops could find no place to hold their ground along the road and retreated all the way into the territory of Tonglu County. Song Jiang advanced through the night and made camp beyond Baifeng Ridge. That night he ordered Xie Zhen, Xie Bao, Yan Shun, Wang Ying, and Hu Sanniang to take the eastern road, while Li Kui, Xiang Chong, Li Gun, Fan Rui, and Ma Lin took the western road. Each party led a thousand infantrymen to raid the camp at Tonglu County. On the river, Li Jun, the three Ruan brothers, the two Tong brothers, and Meng Kang—the seven of them—were ordered to advance by water. Now Xie Zhen and the others led their troops to Tonglu County, arriving in the third watch of the night. The Imperial Preceptor Baoguang was discussing military affairs with Shi Bao when a sudden cannon blast rang out, and everyone scrambled to mount. Looking about in haste, they saw fires rising from three directions. The generals followed Shi Bao and thought only of saving their lives; none dared turn to meet the enemy. The three columns charged in, slashing their way recklessly through everything before them. Wen Kerang was late mounting his horse and fled down a side path, only to run straight into Wang Ying and Hu Sanniang. Husband and wife attacked him together, dragged him from his horse, and took him alive. Li Kui, Xiang Chong, Li Gun, Fan Rui, and Ma Lin devoted themselves to killing and setting fires throughout the county town. When Song Jiang received the report, he hurried his troops forward, struck camp, and moved the entire army to Tonglu County, where they took up their quarters. Wang Ying and Hu Sanniang presented Wen Kerang and claimed credit for his capture. Song Jiang ordered Wen Kerang to be escorted to Commander Zhang in Hangzhou and beheaded before him. Of that, no more need be said.

p.src: The next day, Song Jiang marshaled his forces and advanced by land and water until they reached the foot of Wulong Ridge. Beyond the ridge lay Muzhou. By then, the Imperial Preceptor Baoguang had led all his generals up the ridge to hold the pass and station their troops there. The pass at Wulong Ridge stood close beside the great river. The mountain was steep and the current swift; fortifications crowned the heights, while warships were arrayed below. Song Jiang's army took up position near the foot of the ridge and erected a stockaded camp. From the infantry he sent Li Kui, Xiang Chong, and Li Gun with five hundred shield-bearers to scout the road ahead. When they reached the foot of Wulong Ridge, rolling logs and cannon stones came crashing down from above. Unable to advance and at a loss what to do, they returned to report to Vanguard Song. Song Jiang then sent Ruan Xiao'er, Meng Kang, Tong Meng, and Tong Wei to row half the warships upstream toward the shallows. p.src: These four commanders had originally been boatmen on the Qiantang River. After joining Fang La, they had received offices of the third rank. That day, Ruan Xiao'er and his companions rode their boats against the swift current and rowed upstream toward the shallows. The four commanders in the southern army's naval stockade had already learned of their approach and prepared fifty linked fire rafts. These fire rafts were made by fastening together great pine and fir logs. Bundles of straw were piled upon them, with sulfur, saltpeter, and other combustibles hidden inside; the whole was bound with bamboo rope and arrayed at the head of the shallows. Meanwhile, Ruan Xiao'er, Meng Kang, Tong Wei, and Tong Meng thought only of rowing upstream toward the shallows. The four naval commanders spotted them from above. Each raised a plain red signal flag, boarded one of four swift boats, and rowed downstream with the current. Seeing them, Ruan Xiao'er ordered his sailors to loose arrows, and the four swift boats turned back. Ruan Xiao'er called on his men to seize the advantage and pursue them upstream. The four swift boats drew alongside the shallows and stopped; the four commanders leaped ashore, and the many sailors also fled. Ruan Xiao'er saw how many ships lay within the naval stockade above the shallows and dared not advance farther. While he hesitated, a signal flag suddenly waved atop Wulong Ridge. Gongs and drums sounded together, every fire raft was ignited, and they came hurtling downstream with the wind. Behind them, the crews of the great ships raised a concerted shout and followed close upon the fire rafts, armed with long spears and grappling hooks. Seeing that the onslaught was too fierce to withstand, Tong Wei and Tong Meng brought their boat alongside the bank, abandoned it, clambered around the mountainside, climbed the mountain, and sought a path back to camp. Ruan Xiao'er and Meng Kang, however, remained aboard their ship to meet the enemy. The blazing rafts bore down upon them one after another. As Ruan Xiao'er hurried to leap into the water, a pursuing vessel caught him with a grappling hook. In his panic, Ruan Xiao'er feared he would be captured and humiliated. He drew the saber at his waist and cut his own throat. Meng Kang saw that matters were desperate and was about to plunge into the water when the fire cannons on the rafts all discharged. One shot struck him squarely on the helmet, smashed through the crown, and reduced his head to pulp. The four naval commanders then boarded the fire ships and came killing their way downstream. Li Jun, Ruan Xiaowu, and Ruan Xiaoqi were all aboard the ships in the rear. Seeing the vanguard defeated and the enemy advancing along the riverbank, they had no choice but to turn their vessels in haste and let the current carry them back down toward the bank at Tonglu.

p.src: Song Jiang made camp and raised stockades at Tonglu. Having now lost Ruan Xiao'er and Meng Kang as well, he grieved in his tent, forsaking food and sleep and finding no peace even in his dreams. Wu Yong and the other commanders pleaded earnestly with him, but to no avail. After Ruan Xiaoqi and Ruan Xiaowu had completed their mourning rites, they came of their own accord to remonstrate with Song Jiang: “Our brother has given his life today in the service of the state. That is better than dying obscurely in the Liangshan Marsh, his name buried with him. Commander of the Vanguard, you need not grieve; please attend first to the great affairs of the state. We two brothers will avenge him ourselves.” Hearing this, Song Jiang's expression gradually softened.

p.src: The next day he again mustered and inspected his troops, intending to advance once more. Wu Yong remonstrated: “Brother, you must not be impatient. Let us first think over our strategy again; it will not be too late to cross the ridge afterward.” Then Xie Zhen and Xie Bao said: “We brothers were hunters to begin with and are accustomed to scaling mountains and crossing ridges. We shall disguise ourselves as local hunters, climb the mountain, and set a fire. The bandit troops will be thrown into panic and are sure to abandon the pass.” Wu Yong said: “The plan is good, but I fear the mountain is so steep that you will find it hard to advance. If either of you should lose his footing, your lives could not be saved.” Xie Zhen and Xie Bao replied: “Ever since we broke out of prison in Dengzhou and went up to the Liangshan Marsh, we have enjoyed our brother's protection, lived as heroes for many years, received commissions from the state, and worn brocade coats. If today, for the imperial court, our bones are ground to powder and our bodies smashed to pieces in repayment of our noble brother, it would still be no great sacrifice.” Song Jiang said: “Worthy brothers, do not utter such ominous words. I only hope we shall soon accomplish our great task and return to the capital; the imperial court will surely not treat us unfairly. Devote all your hearts and strength to serving the state.” Xie Zhen and Xie Bao went to make ready. They put on tiger-skin jackets, hung a sharp saber at each waist, and took up their steel-tined forks. The two took leave of Song Jiang, then followed a narrow path up toward Wulong Ridge. It was only the first watch when they encountered two soldiers lying in ambush along the road. They finished the two men off, and by the time they reached the foot of the ridge it was already the second watch. They could clearly hear the watch drum sounding in the stockade atop the ridge. Not daring to take the main road, they clung to vines and creepers and climbed the ridge step by step. That night the moon shone as brightly as day. After climbing two-thirds of the way, they saw lights flickering on the ridge above. The two crouched beside the ridge gate and listened; above them, the drum had already sounded the fourth watch. Xie Zhen quietly called to his brother: “The nights are short, and dawn is not far off. Let us go up.” They began climbing again. They had reached a rugged rock face amid precipitous cliffs. Intent only on climbing, with hands and feet constantly occupied, they had strapped their steel forks beneath their arms and let them trail behind their backs. The forks scraped noisily against bamboo and vines, and someone on the ridge soon spotted them. As Xie Zhen was climbing through a hollow in the mountain, he suddenly heard a shout from above: “Take that!” A hooked pole caught him squarely by his topknot. Xie Zhen hastily reached for the saber at his waist, but by the time he drew it, the men above had already hoisted him up with his feet dangling. In his panic, Xie Zhen swiftly hacked through the hook, only to plunge through the air. Alas, after living half his life as a hero, Xie Zhen fell headlong from a cliff hundreds of feet high and met a violent death. Below lay jagged, fanglike rocks, which smashed his body to pieces. Seeing his elder brother tumble down, Xie Bao hurriedly retreated down the ridge. But rocks large and small were already rolling from above, while bolts and arrows shot through the bamboo and vines. Alas, Xie Bao, a hunter all his life, was shot dead there beside Wulong Ridge amid the bamboo and vines. Thus both brothers perished.

p.src: At daybreak, men were sent down from the ridge to fetch the bodies of Xie Zhen and Xie Bao, which they exposed on the ridge. A scout learned the full particulars and reported to Vanguard Commander Song that Xie Zhen and Xie Bao had died on Wulong Ridge. When Song Jiang heard that Xie Zhen and Xie Bao had also been lost, he wept until he fainted several times. He then summoned Guan Sheng and Hua Rong and ordered troops mustered to seize the pass at Wulong Ridge and avenge his four brothers. Wu Yong remonstrated: “My noble brother, you must not act in haste. The deaths of those already fallen were all ordained by Heaven. If we are to take the pass, we must not proceed rashly. Only after devising an inspired and subtle stratagem and capturing it by cunning may we deploy our troops and commanders.” Song Jiang said angrily: “Who would have thought that a full third of our brothers, as dear as my own limbs, would be lost? I cannot bear to let those bandits expose my brothers' bodies on the ridge. Tonight I must lead troops there first, recover their corpses, and bury them in proper coffins.” Wu Yong tried to stop him: “The bandits have exposed the bodies because they surely have a scheme in mind. Brother, you must not act rashly.” But Song Jiang would not heed the military adviser's remonstrance. He at once mustered three thousand picked troops and, taking the four commanders Guan Sheng, Hua Rong, Lü Fang, and Guo Sheng, advanced through the night. By the time they reached Wulong Ridge, it was already the second watch. A junior officer reported: “Two men have been hung out for exposure ahead. I daresay they are the bodies of Xie Zhen and Xie Bao.” Song Jiang spurred his horse forward to look for himself. From two trees, two bodies had been hoisted on bamboo poles. A patch of bark had been pared from one tree and two lines of large characters written there, but in the moonless darkness he could not make them out.
